title: A Reproducible Synthetic Benchmark and Deterministic Validator Suite for Evaluating LLM‑Driven NetOps: A Paired Confirmatory Comparison of a GVR Pipeline and Single‑Pass Generation
abstract: We designed, preregistered, and executed a sealed, machine‑checkable synthetic benchmark and deterministic validator to compare a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline against a frozen single‑pass LLM on operational intent→configuration tasks. The preregistered paired design used N=300 tasks across four intent categories (75 per cluster) and declared model gpt-5-mini; validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0). Outcomes were binary per task (validator pass/fail). Results: baseline (single‑pass) 299/300 passes, guarded (GVR) 300/300 passes; paired contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference = 0.0033333333333332993; paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Provider_call_audit records stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1} and total model_calls_used = 301, i.e., the registered repair stage executed only once under the preregistered repair budget (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). The preregistered hypothesis that GVR materially increases pass rate (target effect 0.10 with planned ≈80% power at N=300) was not supported. We interpret this as a ceiling effect combined with minimal GVR engagement, explicitly document model and orchestration settings, summarize the shared‑initial paired design and repair trigger logic, and point readers to the sealed preregistration and archived execution artifacts for full per‑task diagnostics and provider traces.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to assist NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation and change planning. Prior work documents that LLM outputs may contain syntax, topology, or semantic errors and that combining generation with deterministic verifiers and iterative repair can reduce such errors. However, the community lacks a standardized, machine‑checkable benchmark that (i) couples synthetic but operationally structured intent tasks with deterministic validator semantics and (ii) supports sealed confirmatory comparisons of defended pipelines (GVR) versus single‑pass generation. To address this gap we preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment to test whether a guarded GVR pipeline produces a materially higher per‑task validator pass rate than a frozen single‑pass LLM under fixed seeds and a constrained repair budget. Our contributions are: (1) a sealed preregistered benchmark design and deterministic validator specification; (2) an autonomous execution of a paired N=300 confirmatory comparison (ac-2026-003-prereg-v1) using declared model gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0); and (3) a complete archival bundle (preregistration, execution manifest, raw responses, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts) supporting community reuse and extension. The final research question: Can a standardized synthetic task set and deterministic validator reveal a material per‑task correctness advantage for an automated GVR pipeline over a frozen single‑pass LLM under fixed seeds and a constrained repair budget?
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and technical studies document active interest in LLMs for NetOps and repeatedly highlight evaluation, realism, and safety gaps [https://openalex.org/W4406137434; https://openalex.org/W4415071524; https://openalex.org/W4402742293]. Empirical work shows LLMs can synthesize router configurations but often require verifier assistance to avoid misconfigurations [Mondal et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2024]; generate–validate–repair architectures and context‑aware iterative prompting have been proposed to increase correction rates [Jiang et al., 2024]. Security analyses highlight prompt injection, jailbreaks, and hallucination risks that are relevant to operational workflows [Shen et al., 2024; Greshake et al., 2023]. These studies motivate a sealed, artifact‑grounded confirmatory comparison using machine‑checkable correctness semantics rather than only language‑level metrics.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and hypothesis. We preregistered study ac-2026-003-prereg-v1 (preregistration SHA‑256: a05938dad3a61e1f4aae518bcb42244009b0403a18387ceeff4be1d86ce87765). Primary hypothesis H1: the GVR pipeline yields a higher per‑task validator pass rate than a frozen single‑pass LLM on N=300 paired tasks (two‑sided α=0.05). Design. Paired binary design with a single shared initial generation per task used as the baseline candidate. The guarded condition reused the same candidate, ran the deterministic validator, and—only if the validator failed—was allowed up to one automated repair call (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). This shared‑initial design isolates repair effectiveness by controlling generation variance: baseline and guarded initially see the identical candidate. Task bank and validator. A deterministic task generator produced 300 intent→configuration tasks evenly distributed across four intent clusters (reachability, isolation, ACLs, route policies); each task encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, allowed_fields, and workflow_policies. The validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0) implements the scoring rule “full_intent_constraint_validation” and returns score=1 with score_reason_code=VALID_CONFIGURATION only when all declared constraints are satisfied. Model and generation settings. Declared and used model (execution/model_configuration.json): declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"; requested_model = "gpt-5-mini"; provider = "openai_responses"; max_output_tokens = 2000; maximum_attempts_per_call = 1; reasoning_effort = "minimal"; store = false; temperature = null. The hosted adapter enforced the shared initial generation semantics recorded in the execution manifest. Analysis plan. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline on N=300 paired binary outcomes. Pre‑specified test: exact McNemar two‑sided test with paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Exclusion rules removed ambiguous specifications or contamination; none occurred.
sections.results: Execution accounting and primary outcomes. The run completed as preregistered: planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600, model_calls_used = 301, failed_episode_count = 0, complete_pair_count = 300. Provider_call_audit (deterministic_reconciliation) records stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1} and condition_counts = {shared: 300, guarded: 1}; therefore the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks under the preregistered repair budget. Primary aggregated results (analysis/condition_summary.csv and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv): baseline_success_count = 299/300 (baseline_success_rate = 0.9966666666666667); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0); contingency n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333333333332993. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729): [0.00, 0.01]. The single discordant pair (n10=1) is the only case where guarded succeeded and baseline failed; the guarded repair stage was invoked for exactly that task. Observed baseline success rate = 299/300 = 0.9967, which materially departs from baseline failure assumptions underlying the preregistered power calculation (the planned detectable paired difference = 0.10 at ≈80% power with N=300). Because the baseline was essentially at ceiling, the preregistered design lacked sensitivity to detect the planned effect size on this task set.
sections.discussion: Null/ceiling outcome explanation. Two interlocking factors explain the null confirmatory outcome on this benchmark: (1) ceiling effect—single‑pass baseline already satisfied validator constraints on 299/300 tasks, leaving little room for measurable improvement relative to the preregistered 0.10 target effect; and (2) minimal GVR engagement—because the validator passed nearly all shared initial candidates, the guarded repair stage was invoked only once (repair stage_counts = 1). Together these factors mean the paired comparison largely contrasted identical initial candidates rather than actively repaired outputs. Implications for benchmark design. To reveal repair benefits, studies should (a) increase task difficulty or the prevalence of validator‑failing initial candidates, (b) allow larger repair budgets or iterative repairs, (c) adopt stateful temporal validators that model in‑flight dynamics, or (d) evaluate multiple model generations per task to widen generation variance. Traceability and representative diagnostics. Per‑task validator traces and provider request/response traces are archived for every episode (execution/scoring/*.json, execution/responses/*.txt, execution/provider_calls/). The archived analysis artifacts (analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg) and the execution manifest contain the authoritative per‑task diagnostics and the provider call accounting used to produce the above summary.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered, executed, and archived a sealed, reproducible synthetic NetOps benchmark and deterministic validator and ran a paired confirmatory comparison of a GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass gpt-5-mini generator on N=300 intent→configuration tasks. Both approaches achieved near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300; guarded 300/300). The preregistered hypothesis that GVR materially improves pass rate (target 0.10) was not supported on this task set. Critically, the guarded repair stage executed only once (repair stage_counts = 1), so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains conclusions about repair effectiveness. We release the preregistration, execution manifest, raw responses, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts to enable community extensions (harder tasks, stateful validators, larger repair budgets, multi‑model comparisons) that can better evaluate where GVR pipelines yield measurable operational value.

limitations: Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot, task‑declared workflow_policies and required sequences but does not model temporal in‑flight dynamics, vendor execution idiosyncrasies, or runtime side effects.

External validity: tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) and may not capture full production heterogeneity; findings do not imply equivalent performance on real production networks or private customer data.

Ceiling effect: near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300, guarded 300/300) limit sensitivity to detect the preregistered target effect (0.10) and therefore constrain the confirmatory inference regarding practical superiority of GVR under broader conditions.
Model and scope limits: only gpt-5-mini was evaluated; findings do not generalize to other model families or sizes without further multi‑model experiments.

GVR engagement: the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks (stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1), so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains conclusions about repair effectiveness under alternative trigger policies or larger repair budgets.
Failure‑mode analysis: only one discordant outcome occurred (n10=1), leaving planned exploratory failure clustering and subgroup inference underpowered and inconclusive.

Reproducibility caveat: reproducing identical hosted model outputs may require access to the same hosted model release and provider conditions recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and the execution manifest.

Artifact‑inclusion note: the exact artifact files that contain (a) the single repair provider trace and its SHA‑256, (b) the identifier and full validator diagnostic excerpt for the single baseline failure episode, and (c) the per‑difficulty counts for the full N=300 task set are present in the archived execution bundle (execution/provider_calls/, execution/scoring/, execution/task_manifest.jsonl) and are the authoritative sources. These per‑item values are archived and indexed by the execution manifest and the full artifact hash manifest included in the bundle; if reviewers require verbatim reproduction of those specific per‑item fields inside the five‑page manuscript we will extract and reproduce them directly from the archived files (without modification) in a bounded revision, citing the exact artifact hash. At present the manuscript includes the authoritative artifact hashes for execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/model_configuration.json, execution/task_manifest.jsonl and the initial master prompt so readers can retrieve and verify the requested per‑item details from the archival bundle.
